name: Guardian genius crossword No 209
preamble: Possible book titles here by whimsically named authors are: 8 by 22 17 3; 22 2 5 by 25 18; 30 by 13 9; and 26 6 by 32 33. All these clues consist only of wordplay.

solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Idiot felt, perhaps, not all there

indicators.note: something not all there is incomplete, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: felt is one example of cloth, hence 'perhaps'

explanation.surface: Someone thinks an idiot has felt a little absent-minded.
explanation.walkthrough: CLOTH loses its last letter to leave CLOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Clot is informal British slang for a stupid person, a dimwit.

clue.text: Little remaining of elder, say, in defeat

blocks.note: first meaning: the short base left when a tree such as an elder is felled
second meaning: to baffle or beat someone

explanation.surface: An older person, reduced to very little, has lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elder' reads as an older person, but it is the elder tree, and 'say' marks it as one example of a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the base of a felled tree trunk and a verb meaning to baffle or get the better of someone.

indicators.note: said briefly, the name is cut short by its final letter
one piece sits by the other, simply placed side by side

blocks.note: another author: Saul Bellow, the American novelist
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: One writer is apprehended by a second writer, briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: BELLOW clipped to BELLO, then C, gives BELLOC; one author's name is built from another's.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilaire Belloc was an Anglo-French writer of verse and essays, so he is an author.

clue.text: River over mountain carrying last of freight in large container

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means placed above, so this piece comes first
the last of a word is its final letter only
something carrying another holds it inside itself
one thing in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: the Don is a river in England and in Russia
an alp is a high mountain
the final letter of freight
a drum is a big cylindrical container

explanation.surface: A river barge's cargo is described: a large drum hauled past a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nest: the mountain carries the drum, which carries the letter. The preamble's title is 'Donald Trump' by Ivor Hugh Jego, i.e. 'I've a huge ego'.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble makes this a book title, the name of the former US president, matched to a joke author name about vanity.

clue.text: A retired author using bold shapes and colours

blocks.note: taken as written
rtd is the standard abbreviation for retired
Umberto Eco, the Italian author of The Name of the Rose

explanation.surface: A writer who has stopped working now paints with strong forms and colours.
explanation.definitionFit: Art deco is the 1920s-30s design style known for bold geometric forms and strong colours, used here as an adjective.

clue.text: Left in dirt I say, dragged around, undesirable

indicators.note: one thing in another is enclosed by it
dragged round, the string is turned to face the other way

blocks.note: mud is wet dirt
L is the abbreviation for left
an exclamation of surprise, like 'I say!'

explanation.surface: Someone left in the dirt, dragged about by an unwelcome type, protests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I say' is a British exclamation of surprise; 'dragged around' applies to everything built before it, not just the last piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An undesirable, used as a noun, is an objectionable person, and a hoodlum is a violent petty criminal.

clue.text: One of a couple cheering in style

blocks.note: first meaning: one of the pair of words in the cheer '... ... hooray'
second meaning: fashionable, trendy

explanation.surface: One half of a pair cheers while dressed fashionably.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheer goes 'hip, hip, hooray', with two of the word, and the word is also slang for fashionable.

clue.text: French city hotel refurbished sovereign's office containing ultimate in chinoiserie

indicators.note: a refurbished building is done over and rearranged
the ultimate in a word is its very last letter
one piece containing another holds it inside

blocks.note: Pau is a city in south-west France
the letters to rearrange
the throne stands for a monarch's position
the final letter of chinoiserie

explanation.surface: A hotel in a French city is redone, and the royal suite gets oriental décor.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble's title is 'Go On' by Paul the Other One, i.e. 'pull the other one', the British retort meaning 'I don't believe you'. Paul is also the setter.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble supplies this joke author name, a pun on the sceptical idiom 'pull the other one' answering the title.

indicators.note: picking at regular intervals takes every other letter

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of spheral

explanation.surface: A round vegetable is gathered from the garden at intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is apt: the seed is spherical and is picked. Take letters 2, 4 and 6.
explanation.definitionFit: The pea is a climbing leguminous plant grown for its round edible seeds.

clue.text: New is up against old leader

indicators.note: a new version of the words is a fresh arrangement of their letters

blocks.note: the two words supply the letters to rearrange
v is short for versus, meaning against

explanation.surface: A fresh challenger has risen against the former chief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' reads as an adjective in the surface, but it is the signal to rearrange 'is up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pius V was the sixteenth-century pope, so a leader of the Catholic Church from long ago.

clue.text: Competitive round after round in VW drophead coupé?

blocks.note: first meaning: rounds of ... played in an ... championship
second meaning: a convertible version of the Volkswagen hatchback model

explanation.surface: Racing lap after lap in a convertible Volkswagen.
explanation.walkthrough: A drophead is a car with a folding roof, so an open car; the Golf is a Volkswagen model, and the Open is golf's oldest championship.
explanation.definitionFit: Golf played in the Open championship is competitive, and a soft-top VW Golf is an open Golf.

clue.text: Parasite accordingly on foot of patient

indicators.note: one piece placed on another is simply followed by it
the foot of a word is its bottom, the last letter

blocks.note: ergo is Latin for therefore, accordingly
the final letter of patient

explanation.surface: A parasite has, as a result, got onto a sick person's foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergot is a parasitic fungus that infects rye and other cereals.

clue.text: After initial loss, South African rugby reaching high point in Australia

indicators.note: losing the initial means the first letter is dropped
one piece reaching another runs straight on into it

blocks.note: the Zulu are a South African people
RU is short for rugby union

explanation.surface: A South African rugby side, after an early defeat, climbs to the top in Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Uluru, once called Ayers Rock, is the huge sandstone monolith rising from the Australian outback.

clue.text: A little pseudo-Homeric expression of frustration

indicators.note: a little of the following text means just a part of it is taken

blocks.note: spans the end of pseudo and the start of Homeric

explanation.surface: A short mock-epic cry of annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Homeric' is a nod to Homer Simpson, whose catchphrase this is.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer Simpson's catchphrase is the exclamation of exasperation at one's own stupidity.

indicators.note: less something means without it, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: TT means teetotal, so dry
a piggy person eats greedily, like a glutton

explanation.surface: A slightly damper particle of something pig-related.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less dry' looks like a comparative adjective; it is 'dry' removed from the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: The gluon is the subatomic particle that carries the strong force binding quarks together.

clue.text: Short key, article lost in pilgrimage, in great journey

indicators.note: cut short, the word loses its final letter
something lost from a word is taken out of it
one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: a piano key is an ivory
great in size
the haj is the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca
a is the indefinite article
to go is to journey

explanation.surface: A short note on a pilgrimage that turned into a great journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' is a piano key, named after the material it was made of. Said aloud the name is 'I've a huge ego', the author of 'Donald Trump'.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble makes this the joke author name of the book 'Donald Trump', a pun on boasting vanity.

indicators.note: something novel is new, a fresh arrangement of the letters

blocks.note: every letter of these three words is used

explanation.surface: A reader conquers a dreadful book.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, the author name is 'I've a sore beach bum' (bum is British slang for backside), writing 'Sandy Knickers'. 'Novel' looks like the book itself; it is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble makes this the joke author name for the book 'Sandy Knickers', a pun about chafing at the seaside.

definitions.note: a noun phrase: the thing that is dreary, a dull routine

indicators.note: cut short, the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: Ruth is a book of the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A brief volume that is tedious.
explanation.definitionFit: A rut is a dull, monotonous routine one is stuck in, something tedious.

indicators.note: shaving takes a little off each side, so both ends go

blocks.note: a chick is a baby bird

explanation.surface: A tipsy man nicks himself shaving and confesses he is drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baby' reads as an endearment; it is a baby bird with both ends trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Hic represents a hiccup, the sound comic writing gives a drunk person.

indicators.note: one piece taking another picks it up to carry alongside
something put into another goes inside it

blocks.note: Prince Andrew, known as Andy
K is the chess abbreviation for king
Snickers is a chocolate bar

explanation.surface: A prince brings the king into a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub; it is the chocolate bar, split after its S. Knickers are British for underpants; this is the book by 'I've a sore beach bum'.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble makes this a book title, sandy underwear, paired with the pun author name about a sore seat.

clue.text: Figure under a wing buffeted about

indicators.note: being buffeted about means being knocked into a jumbled new order
in a down clue, under means placed below, so this piece comes after

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
eight is a figure, a number

explanation.surface: A shape tossed about beneath a plane's wing.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble's title 'Gain Weight' is by Duncan Donuts, a pun on the Dunkin' Donuts chain.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble makes this a book title, getting heavier, paired with an author named after a doughnut chain.

clue.text: One's awfully tired of dull arty wife

definitions.text: One's awfully tired of dull arty wife

blocks.clueFragment: One's awfully tired of dull arty wife
blocks.note: surface reading: a man is sick of his boring, pretentious wife

blocks.clueFragment: awfully tired of dull arty wife
blocks.note: setter's reading: 'awfully tired' uses exactly the letters of 'dull arty wife', and the clue says it is one of those

explanation.surface: A husband is fed up with his dreary, arty wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Count the letters: 'awfully tired' and 'dull arty wife' are the same twelve letters rearranged, so 'One' is the kind of wordplay this is.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of another, as these two phrases are.

blocks.note: first meaning: authentic, not fake
second meaning: an old Spanish silver coin, also Brazil's currency

explanation.definitionFit: The word means authentic, and is also a historic Spanish coin and the Brazilian currency unit.

clue.text: Encapsulating allure, what spirit doing a twirl in loose garment

indicators.note: encapsulating something means holding it inside a capsule
a twirl turns the whole string round to face the other way

blocks.note: eh is a 'what?' asking someone to repeat
it means sex appeal, as in the 'It girl'
gin is a spirit

explanation.surface: An alluring ghost twirls about in a flowing dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' suggests a ghost, but it is the drink; the twirl turns round everything built before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightie is a loose nightdress, a garment worn to bed.

blocks.note: the answer at 31 means a thug

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is just a cross-reference: a synonym of 31's answer, split as two words. The preamble's title 'Go On' is by Paul the Other One.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble makes this a book title, the sceptical 'go on!', answered by the author name meaning 'pull the other one'.

indicators.note: the word before it is not there, so its letters are taken away

blocks.note: Ted Hughes, Poet Laureate 1984-98, written T Hughes
the contraction gives three letters to remove

explanation.surface: A hoodlum is plainly no Poet Laureate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He's not' reads as an aside about the hoodlum; it is the instruction to remove HES from T HUGHES.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer to 11, a hoodlum, is a violent criminal, which is what a thug is.

clue.text: Horse far from stable maintaining positive attitude

indicators.note: to maintain something here is to keep it held within

blocks.note: a dun is a greyish-brown horse
mentally far from stable, i.e. crazy
a can-do attitude is a positive one

explanation.surface: A horse that has bolted from its stable still keeps its spirits up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Far from stable' reads as a horse out of its stable; it means mentally unstable. Said aloud the name sounds like the Dunkin' Donuts chain, author of 'Gain Weight'.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble makes this the joke author name of 'Gain Weight', a nod to the doughnut chain.
